title: MLflow and Unity Catalog model registries

opening.headline: We explain the reason why the operational service continues to use the previous version after changing the model version by examining the way the model is referenced.
body: Although a new model version has been registered and verified in the registry, the operational service continues to respond using the previous version. This is because the service code references the model using a fixed version number. In this case, to use the new version, the code must be modified and redeployed.

In this lesson, we examine the relationship between MLflow Tracking and Unity Catalog Model Registry, comparing how version numbers and aliases differ. We then review the workflow of migrating an alias to deploy a new version into production, and explore a case study of refactoring a service that hardcodes version numbers to instead reference versions via aliases.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the relationship between MLflow tracking and Unity Catalog model registry, aliases
You can distinguish between version number references and alias references.

screens.title: We changed the model version, but the operational service is still using the previous version.
screens.lead: This is a common scenario during the model promotion process. You can check what the issue is by selecting each item.

visual.alt: The registry contains version 2 registered, but the operational service loads the fixed version 1 in the code.

items.prompt: Version 2 has been newly registered in the registry.
items.answer: When a new version is registered, version 2 appears in the registry. However, registration only preserves the model; it does not change which version receives operational traffic.

items.prompt: The operational service code contains a version number, such as models:/prod.ml_team.iris_model/1.
items.answer: The `/1` appended to the load address fixes the version that the service will load. As long as this value does not change, the service ignores any new versions that may be created in the registry.

items.prompt: Even after updating to a new version, the service continues to respond with version 1.
items.answer: The model is properly registered, but since the service behavior hasn't changed, it appears as a failure—actually, this is a problem related to the reference mechanism. The root of the inconvenience lies in the fact that upgrades and rollbacks are tightly coupled with code modifications and redeployment.

screens.outro: The question for this class is this: What should be the model reference that services are looking toward?

screens.title: Preview: Model Version Reference
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Please think about the answer mentally before entering or submitting it.

items.prompt: How do I reference a model version?
items.answer: It's common to hardcode file paths or version numbers into code or configurations. While numbers are precise and simple, they require manual updates every time they change.

items.prompt: When deploying a new version, should you modify the code and redeploy it again?
items.answer: If the code is modified and redeployed, then model changes will follow the same procedure as code deployments. In AI services where model updates are frequent, this process becomes burdensome, and the risk of accidentally specifying the wrong version increases.

items.prompt: If we need to roll back to a previous version, what should be changed?
items.answer: In a service where the version number is fixed, you must modify and redeploy the code again. Rollbacks are performed only in emergencies, so the procedure should be lightweight and quick. Check how to reduce this process to a single step in the following screen.

screens.outro: First, we will verify the relationship between the two tools for recording and registering models.

screens.title: MLflow Tracking and Unity Catalog Model Registry
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to walk through the process step by step, starting from when the learning execution is recorded and the model is registered in the registry.

visual.alt: Flow diagram showing learning execution recorded in MLflow and registered as a model version in Unity Catalog.

steps.title: MLflow tracking records executions.
steps.body: MLflow Tracking is an API and UI that records parameters, code versions, metrics, and output files when executing machine learning code, enabling comparison on screen later. Each execution of `python train.py` constitutes one run, and each run retains metrics and parameters, start and end times, and other outputs such as model weights.

steps.title: Unity Catalog provides a model registry.
steps.body: Databricks provides MLflow Model Registry hosted within Unity Catalog. Benefits of Unity Catalog such as centralized access control, auditing, lineage, and model search across workspaces are applied. It is also compatible with the open-source MLflow Python client.

steps.title: The model name is written in three steps.
steps.body: In Unity Catalog, models are registered with a three-part name in the format `catalog.schema.model`. The example from this class is `iris_model`, located in the `ml_team` schema of the `prod` catalog. When calling `log_model`, passing the name to `registered_model_name` registers the model during training, and a new version is created each time it is registered.

steps.title: Keep signature and input example together
steps.body: New model versions in Unity Catalog must have a model signature. When logging, providing input examples automatically infers the signature, recording the input and output formats of the model. A signature ensures errors are reported when inputs during inference do not match.

steps.title: The table used for learning is traceable by lineage.
steps.body: If you trained a model using tables in Unity Catalog, you can save the input table information to `mlflow.log_input`. Once the model is registered, this lineage information is automatically saved and can be viewed in the Lineage tab of the model version page.

steps.title: The model is a security target and permissions are managed with GRANT.
steps.body: Models registered in Unity Catalog are security targets of type `FUNCTION`. Therefore, access permissions are granted using `GRANT`. To create a new model, you need the `CREATE MODEL` and `USE SCHEMA` schema permissions, as well as the `USE CATALOG` catalog permission.

screens.outro: Let's compare how an alias fills in the gaps where version numbers alone are insufficient.

screens.title: Version number and alias, distinction between environment and deployment status
screens.lead: Compare the version number, alias, catalog, and schema in the table below to see what each represents.

visual.alt: A diagram showing the relationship between fixed version numbers and movable aliases.

data.caption: Three nameplates indicating the model

This does not change and is the number attached to the model content.
A mutable name referring to a specific version and indicating the deployment status
You can move it to another version.
This represents the environment and governance rules in which the model operates.

Number requires code modification and alias can only be changed by relocation.
data.notes: The fact that a model version is listed in the `prod` catalog does not mean that it is receiving production traffic. Catalogs, schemas, and registered models reflect only the environment (`prod`) and governance rules, not the deployment status. For example, administrators can be granted permissions to delete entries only from the `prod` catalog. The deployment status is managed via an alias. To set an alias, a user must be the owner of the registered model and have the `USE SCHEMA` permission on the schema and the `USE CATALOG` permission on the catalog.

screens.outro: I'll take a look at the code that actually moves and invokes aliases.

screens.title: alias promotion flow and loading URI
screens.lead: This is the code that promotes and loads a model using an alias. Please check the symptoms when the line numbers in the right-side explanation do not align.

visual.alt: Champion alias moved from version 1 to version 2, with the service flowing to the new version without any code changes.

data.code:
from mlflow import MlflowClient
import mlflow.pyfunc

client = MlflowClient()
name = "prod.ml_team.iris_model"

#Version 1 is designated as the operating version.
client.set_registered_model_alias(name, "Champion", 1)
#Promotion: Move Champion to version 2
client.set_registered_model_alias(name, "Champion", 2)

#The service code loads the model via an alias.
model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(f"models:/{name}@Champion")
#Query the version that Champion is pointing to.
current = client.get_model_version_by_alias(name, "Champion")
#Rollback: moves or deletes an alias to the previous version
client.set_registered_model_alias(name, "Champion", 1)
client.delete_registered_model_alias(name, "Champion")

notes.note: `set_registered_model_alias` attaches an alias to a specific version. If the same alias is called again, it is migrated to another version, so promotion is complete in a single call. This operation requires model owner permissions; if permissions are not granted, the call is rejected.

The loading address is in the format `models:/name@Champion`. Instead of using a number, if you use an alias after `@`, the batching inference job will automatically fetch a new Champion on the next execution, separating model deployment from inference code. If the alias does not exist, an error occurs when trying to locate the model.

`get_model_version_by_alias` queries the version pointed to by the current alias. In deployment flows where it does not automatically follow like a serving endpoint, the queried result is used to update the endpoint's serving version.

Rollback refers to either moving an alias back to its previous version or deleting the alias. The version itself remains in the registry. When an alias is deleted, the service that was previously accessed through that alias will fail to find its model, so it is necessary to verify which service is referencing the alias prior to deletion.

screens.outro: Now, let's walk through an example of refactoring a service that had version numbers hardcoded, to use alias references instead.

screens.title: Analysis: Problems with a service that hardcodes version numbers
screens.lead: The instructor demonstrates the process of replacing a service with a fixed version number using an alias reference. Please follow along by selecting the right-arrow.

visual.alt: A screen displaying side by side the code that calls a model by number and the code that calls it by alias.

steps.title: Step 1: The address for loading is fixed with a number.
steps.body: The loading address of the service code is `models:/prod.ml_team.iris_model/1`. The terminating address `/1` permanently fixes the version of the service that is called. The service continues to load only version 1, unaware that a different version exists.

steps.title: Step 2: Registration and verification of the new version have no impact.
steps.body: The team has registered and verified version 2. However, since the service has fixed the number, there is no impact. Registration and verification have been completed, but the discrepancy in operations remains a symptom of this case.

steps.title: Step 3: You need to modify the code and redeploy it, and the rollback process is the same.
steps.body: To use the new version, you must change the address number to 2 and then redeploy the service. When issues occur and you need to roll back, you must revert the number to 1 and redeploy again. Model upgrades and rollbacks are tightly coupled with code deployments, making them slow and error-prone during urgent situations.

steps.title: Step 4: Change the loading address to @Champion
steps.body: Change the load address to `models:/prod.ml_team.iris_model@Champion`. The service now looks at the label rather than the number. The version to which the label is attached is changed only in the registry, and the service code no longer needs to be modified.

steps.title: Step 5: Handle promotions and demotions as alias movements.
steps.body: Promotion is completed in a single call by moving the Champion to version 2 using `set_registered_model_alias`. If an issue occurs, the Champion is rolled back to version 1 in the same call. Batch inference retrieves a new Champion on the next execution, and the serving endpoint updates the served version after checking the current Champion.

steps.title: Step 6: Separate and manage aliases from access permissions.
steps.body: To set an alias, a user must be the model owner and have permissions on both the schema and catalog. Conversely, a service that retrieves a model via an alias only needs `EXECUTE` permission and `USE SCHEMA`, `USE CATALOG` permissions. Permissions for who can promote and who can retrieve can be managed separately.

screens.outro: Finally, I will summarize the lecture content.

screens.title: Core takeaway: Operation looks at aliases
screens.lead: This course content is organized into recording, registration, referencing, promotion, and return processes.

paragraphs: **Logging and Registration**: MLflow tracking records the execution parameters, metrics, and artifacts, while Unity Catalog Model Registry manages models and versions under the name `catalog.schema.model`. Environments and governance are represented by the catalog and schema, and deployment status is indicated by the alias.

**Reference style**: The version number is fixed, while the alias can be changed. If a service refers to the version number, it will not change even if a new version is released; however, if it refers to the alias, it will automatically follow changes through alias redirection. The loading address is specified in `@alias` format.

**Promotion and Regression**: Promotion involves moving an alias to a new version, while regression involves moving it back to a previous version. This process is handled without modifying the service code or re-deploying, and the version itself remains unchanged in the registry.

glossary.def: This feature records and compares experiment parameters, metrics, and output files.
This is a repository that manages registered models and versions. Unity Catalog identifies them by the catalog.schema.model name.
A fixed number that increments by one each time a model is registered.
A mutable name that refers to a specific model version. Champion is a typical example, indicating the deployment status.

misconceptions.myth: The model in the product catalog is the model currently in operation.
misconceptions.fact: Catalogs and schemas represent environment and governance rules only; they do not represent deployment status. Deployment status is expressed using an alias.

misconceptions.myth: When a new version is registered, the service is automatically updated.
misconceptions.fact: If a service fixes a model using a version number, updating to a new version will have no effect. Only services that watch aliases follow alias moves.

misconceptions.myth: Using an alias deletes the previous version.
misconceptions.fact: An alias is merely a label attached to a version. Moving or deleting an alias does not affect the version's presence in the registry.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Promotion is the act of moving an alias to a new version.
The load address is specified in @alias format.
The environment is represented by a catalog, and the deployment state is represented by an alias.
